results.corrected_extracted: Post-marketing surveillance by an independent steering committee that the drug's sponsor, Ortho-McNeil Pharmaceuticals, set up on the recommendation of the FDA's Drug Abuse Advisory Committee when tramadol (Ultram) was marketed in the USA without scheduling. Reports came from spontaneous adverse-event reports to the company and the FDA (MedWatch: patients, pharmacists, physicians) and from a network of 110 NIDA-funded researchers and 145 other experts on drug use with access to about 250,000 people at risk for drug misuse, offered $75 for each completed questionnaire (average response 48.7% over 20 quarters); a subcommittee classified every report with DSM-IV-based ratings. No group of people who stopped tramadol without withdrawal, or who stopped another opioid, was studied (editors' reading of the design).
results.note: Numbers confirmed on the page (110, 145, 250,000, $75, 48.7%, 20 quarters). The paper calls Ortho-McNeil the sponsor of Ultram, never its manufacturer (p. 234); 'without scheduling' is on p. 233.

results.corrected_extracted: Withdrawal ratings (21 typical, 22 atypical) were used only when there was no drug-seeking or other evidence of 'abuse'; reports with withdrawal and drug-seeking were rated as 'abuse'. Because unusual symptoms appeared as the study progressed, all withdrawal cases of 1995–2000 were rescored as typical or atypical. Typical withdrawal needed at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms; atypical withdrawal also had a strong component of other CNS disturbances, and is described as always accompanied by typical symptoms (3.1), as often combined with them (Table 2, footnote b) and, in the Discussion (p. 238), as occurring in addition to or in place of them. The authors say 'atypical' is a descriptor, not a claim that there are two syndromes. No check of agreement between raters is reported.
results.corrected_locator: 2.2 Detailed methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 235, the 5th continuing p. 236); Table 1 (p. 235); Table 2, footnotes a and b, and 3.1, 1st paragraph (p. 236); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 238)
results.note: Text confirmed unchanged; only page and locator completed, because the 'in addition to or in place of' wording sits in the Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 238), which the locator omitted.

results.corrected_extracted: The abstract says withdrawal of either type made up nearly 40% of all adverse events reported, and the Discussion calls it the most prevalent adverse event (nearly 40% of total cases); Table 3 gives 33%, and 644 of the same 1,248 reports were rated as 'abuse' (3.2, p. 237).
results.corrected_locator: Abstract (p. 233); Table 3 and 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 237); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 238)
results.note: Text confirmed unchanged; locator completed with Table 3 and 3.2 (p. 237), which the text cites. The paper does not say outright that the 644 are among the 1,248, but adds them within 'this study'.

results.corrected_extracted: Typical withdrawal symptoms listed: abdominal cramps, anxiety, bone pain, depression, diarrhoea, goose flesh, insomnia, tearing, nausea, restlessness, runny nose and sweating (no frequencies). Among the 55 atypical cases: severe anxiety and panic attacks 32.8%; unusual CNS symptoms (confusion, delusions, depersonalization, derealization, paranoia) 27.2%; unusual sensory phenomena (numbness, tingling, paresthesia, tinnitus) 25.4%; hallucinations (tactile, visual, auditory) 20.0%; the total exceeds 100% because several were reported together. Editors' calculation: the nearest counts of 55 (18, 15, 14 and 11) give 32.7%, 27.3%, 25.5% and 20.0% when rounded, or 32.7%, 27.2%, 25.4% and 20.0% when cut off; no single rule gives all four printed percentages, so they cannot all come from 55.
results.note: Table 2 values confirmed on the page. Recomputed: cut off instead of rounded, 15/55 and 14/55 give the printed 27.2% and 25.4%; only 32.8% fits neither way, so 'three cannot come from 55' overstated it.
3.2: 644 abuse-rated reports, withdrawal symptoms in 121 (typical) and 3 (atypical); 'at least 546' is the authors' figure. Recomputed 422 + 124 = 546; 546/1248 = 43.75%, 43.8%.

results.corrected_extracted: Age was known for only 139 of 455 withdrawal cases (a total that matches neither 422 nor 546), with no figures given; sex was known in 82% of typical and 87% of atypical cases, of whom about 56% were women (55.8% and 56.3%); the authors say this suggests both types may be more common in women, but that the data do not appear to establish any relation between sex and withdrawal.
results.note: All numbers confirmed (3.3, p. 237). The authors first say the data suggest both types may be more common in women, then that the data 'do not appear to establish' a relation; suggestion and hedge restored.

results.corrected_extracted: Length of exposure was known in about 50% of withdrawal cases: many followed brief exposures of 3–4 days, with no clustering after long exposure (no counts). Maintenance dose was known in 63% of typical cases (50–2,000 mg a day; 92% at or below the maximum recommended level of 400 mg a day) and 78% of atypical cases (50–1,300 mg a day); the paper gives 25% of all atypical cases as above 400 mg, three times the 8% of typical cases, without saying whether the base is all atypical cases or those with a known dose (no counts or test). Atypical cases tended to last longer and to be harder to manage.
results.note: All figures confirmed (pp. 237–238). The paper says 25% 'of all atypical cases', so the base is left open instead of being placed inside the 78% with a known dose.

results.corrected_extracted: Withdrawal followed abrupt discontinuation, which the authors say many physicians did despite the label's warning, and in some instances dose reductions or a tapered stop. Most physicians described relatively mild cases that they monitored without treatment and that usually resolved in 2 or 3 days; as severity increased, treatment was often necessary. The committee's clinicians drew on about 75 consultations; no counts are given, and outcomes only in general terms.
results.note: 3.5 says treatment was 'often necessary' as severity increased (hedge restored). Outcomes are given in general words (resolved in 2–3 days; most atypical symptoms responded), so 'no outcomes' was too strong; treatment details deliberately not added.
2.3 exposure algorithm and all rate statements confirmed. Figure 1 at 300 dpi: typical counts sum to 367, atypical to 55; May 1996 quarter 37 and 10, total plotted about 2.27; last quarter about 0.3.
Discussion, 8th paragraph (pp. 239–240): FDA estimate of about 10% (Kessler, 1993); after several years 'probably' considerably less than 5%, as stated.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors say the atypical symptoms were more like those reported on stopping SSRI antidepressants than on stopping opioids, may relate to tramadol's reported noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition, which remains to be determined, and could be misdiagnosed as psychosis or delirium. They report no difference between typical and atypical cases in age, sex, length of exposure or history of drug misuse (figures shown only for sex), so they could define no feature that would indicate who may be at risk of atypical symptoms, with one possible exception: more atypical cases had been at doses above 400 mg a day (25% against 8%).
results.note: The paper says 'with one possible exception' (hedge restored). Age and length of exposure, like history, have no typical-versus-atypical figures (3.3, 3.4), so 'the last without data shown' became 'figures shown only for sex'.

key_findings.correction: Reports came from two sources: spontaneous reports received by the drug's sponsor, Ortho-McNeil, from patients, pharmacists, physicians and the FDA (MedWatch), and a key-informant network of 110 NIDA grantees and 145 other experts with access to about 250,000 people at risk for misuse, offered $75 per completed questionnaire; the average informant response rate over the 20 quarters was 48.7%.

Age was known for only 139 of 455 withdrawal cases (no figures given; the authors say the ages appear to indicate that age is not an important predisposing factor). Sex was known in 82% of typical and 87% of atypical cases; about 56% were women (55.8% and 56.3%).

Length of exposure was known in about 50% of withdrawal cases and was a weak factor: many cases followed relatively brief exposures of 3–4 days, with no clustering after long exposure (no counts). Maintenance dose was known in 63% of typical cases (range 50–2000 mg per day; 92% at or below 400 mg per day) and 78% of atypical cases (range 50–1300 mg per day); the paper gives 25% of all atypical cases as above 400 mg per day, about three times the 8% of typical cases, without saying whether the base is all atypical cases or those with a known dose. Atypical cases tended to last longer and to be harder to manage.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The abstract (p. 233) and Discussion (p. 238) say withdrawal made up nearly 40% of all adverse events; Table 3 gives 422 of 1248, printed as 33% (editors' arithmetic: 33.8%). | consequence: The 'nearly 40%' matches neither count (33.8% of reports rated withdrawal; 43.8% if the 124 abuse-rated reports with withdrawal symptoms are added), so it is not simply an overstatement; a claim should use one of these with its basis stated.

issue: The text says both kinds of withdrawal may be more common in women, then that the data do not appear to establish any relation with sex (p. 237); no figures for the sex of people prescribed tramadol are given. | consequence: The 56% of women among reported cases cannot be read as a higher risk in women.

risk_of_bias.note: Design (case series), JBI-prevalence domains and overall high agreed. METHODS §5.3 lists no instrument for case series; the JBI domains follow existing case-series cards and each judgment fits the paper.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed. results_show should not say 'per quarter ... in the first year': the paper gives no time unit (the card's own RI1) and the peak came 12–15 months after launch. The management advice has outcomes in general words, not none.

missed: The Discussion says withdrawal could serve as a factor leading to abuse (p. 238) and then that withdrawal without drug-seeking has little or no relationship to abuse (p. 239); the card cites only the second.

The Discussion calls withdrawal a prominent and common feature of a large number of people rated positive for abuse (p. 238); 3.2 gives 124 of 644 positive, possible or alleged abuse reports (19%, editors' calculation; p. 237).
The Ultram label of the time warned of typical but not atypical withdrawal (Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 238).
design_detail and funding.affiliations_note call Ortho-McNeil 'the manufacturer'; the paper calls it the sponsor of Ultram (p. 234).
analysis.effect_sizes gives the 25% above 400 mg as a share of atypical cases with dose data; the paper says 25% of all atypical cases (p. 238).
